rv.q: As the imperious, spurned, fright-bewigged, sweaty glitterbomb at the heart of Hedwig and the Angry Inch, Harris makes Broadway rock harder than it ever has before.
That's the kind of rock-star performance he gives in this spectacular revival — helmed with fabulous flash by Michael Mayer
In the meantime, miss Harris at your peril.
That’s a bona fide Broadway star, the kind who can rule an audience with the blink of a sequined eyelid.
The pertinent answers are that the unlikely Broadway show and its equally unlikely star are doing splendidly.
Before our eyes, Harris is opening another chapter in his exceptional show business career with this 90-minute show and he simply crushes it, holding nothing back, softening no edges, making no nice.
If the current incarnation is a superb rendition of a furiously entertaining show with a heartwarming message
His boots and the show are much kinkier than anything else on Broadway.
Adding to our enjoyment are Hedwig’s fanciful costumes, which were designed by Arianne Phillips.
Only when he finally clicks with the material — as on the heartbreaking “Wig in a Box,” about the process of becoming someone else — is the show suddenly worth the effort he’s poured into it.
Mitchell proves that sometimes you can go home again
Lean and mean NPH throws himself into the role and against the walls with reckless flip-your-wig and in-your-face abandonment.
This Hedwig serves that spirit with a stark exuberance that will stick to you.
'Hedwig and the Angry Inch' is still the finest musical you're going to see this year about a transgendered Berliner with a chip on her shoulder.
As Hedwig, a (mostly) transgendered East German rock singer, he gives one of the Broadway season's fiercest, most compelling – and funniest — portrayals.

The new setting affects the show’s credibility. Would a strange, struggling performer really be invited to perform on a Broadway stage? But as it is, this remains a wildly enjoyable production of one of the most exciting and inventive rock musicals of all time.

He goes for the Ziggy Stardust/David Bowie glam that inspires Hedwig, and so turns Mitchell and Trask’s little tuner into a big Broadway extravaganza that burns as hot as a bruised bottom after an especially rough night of S&M sex.
In that case this production succeeded madly, but I myself was more shell shocked than blown away.
Harris's unstoppable Hedwig will no doubt go on to a magnificent career and the cover of Rolling Stone.

cn.t: Critics hail this Broadway revival as a spectacular triumph, with Neil Patrick Harris delivering a fierce, electrifying performance that's both hilarious and heartbreaking, backed by Michael Mayer's flashy direction and the show's glam-rock energy.

sg.ra: Belasco was designed by David Belasco as a 'living room' with a shallow depth to support the Little Theater movement's emphasis on actor-audience proximity. Center Orchestra rows B-D sit at the ideal distance (reviewers cite row B as the fourth row from stage at 'perfect distance') with head-on actor views. Mezzanine overhang begins at row J per SeatPlan, so rows BB-H stay clear.

SeatPlan confirms 'The Mezzanine overhang begins at row J, meaning seats behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Rows J-Q trade top-of-stage visibility for lower prices. Headout and TickPick both flag G-P/F-O center as value picks. Row N's extra legroom offsets the overhang compromise for tall patrons.

SeatPlan: 'Seats at the Left and Right edges suffer from restricted views of the stage,' particularly corner seats in rows B-E. TickPick confirms 'Far Left/Right Orchestra: Angled views may occur.' Historic box configuration and shallow house geometry amplify side-angle distortion.

sg.vl: Aerial sweet spot, skip row A
sg.ra: Mezzanine hangs close and center row C delivers aerial perspective with decent rake. Row A is a common trap: 'Mezzanine row A seat 111 was obstructed view, and the rail literally blocks half of the stage' (Tripadvisor user report). Balcony overhang begins at mezz row C per SeatPlan, so rows A-B stay open-topped but row A's safety bar offsets that benefit.

Headout flags F-H center as the mezzanine value range. Balcony overhang starting at row C means rows E-H sit under it — top of set may be cut. Side mezzanine suffers progressively more restricted angles 'due to stage curvature' (SeatPlan). Acceptable for dialogue-heavy work but not flown spectacle.

Center Balcony 'extends back six rows on a steep rake which provides a bird's-eye-view of the stage' (SeatPlan). Rows B-D balance price and sightline. Distance is the honest tradeoff: AVFMS reviewer on Maybe Happy Ending noted 'the real problem is how far back the balcony is. You'll have to lean forward to see for most of the show.' Row A safety rail can also obstruct.

sg.vl: Up to 1/3 of stage cut off
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'the curve of the section and other features including the Left Boxes may cut off up to a third of the stage at the outside.' Combined with steep rake, distance, and row A rail, side balcony is the worst seat class in the house. Historic 1907 box architecture is the root cause — it cannot be engineered out per production.
